body: The power goes at twenty past ten on a Sunday morning, in a leisure centre hall with the badminton lines still on the floor. Not all of it — the strip lights stay on — but the desk, the amps and the guitarist’s tuner all die inside the same half second, in the middle of the second verse. About sixty people are standing. For a moment nobody does anything. Then a woman near the back, who has never sung anything on her own in her life, simply keeps going, because she was already halfway through a line and stopping felt ruder than continuing. By the fourth word about half the room is with her, in a key nobody chose, and it is not tidy, and nobody looks at anybody else.

What was in that hall for the next ninety seconds was the song. Everything before the breaker tripped had been the song plus a great deal else, and not one person in the room could have told you where the join was.

Modern worship production is very good, and that is the difficulty. A build, a drop and the right reverb can make almost any line feel significant. The feeling is entirely real. What is not reliable is the inference that the line caused it.

It is worth taking the word production literally for a moment. Compression, sidechain, the reverb tail, the octave doubling on the last chorus, the drop that arrives a bar later than the body expects — these are not decoration. They are techniques for acting directly on a listener, on the breath and the heart rate and the sense of scale, and they work on people who have no idea they are being worked on. That is a craft, not a scandal. But it means that when a line lands, you cannot tell from the inside how much of the landing belonged to the line. Production can make a weak line feel enormous. Take it away and the line has to be enormous by itself, or it is just a sentence.

That is why unaccompanied singing has a place on this band, and not merely as taste. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air, and the catalogue behind them is held to a standard that can only be applied with the arrangement switched off.

Applying it costs something, because a great many songs fail it. Strip the production from a track that works perfectly well in a Sunday set and you will often find a line that turns out to be a placeholder — a phrase in roughly the right shape, holding a slot until the build arrives. That is an uncomfortable thing to discover about material you have loved and sung and meant. It is done anyway, because a catalogue that has never been tested unaccompanied is a catalogue nobody has actually read.

The pressure runs the other way in most places, and not out of cynicism. Songs are now written with the arrangement in mind, because that is how they will be heard, and a line written to sit under a build does not have to survive on its own. Over a few years that lowers the required strength of a line without anybody deciding to lower it. Nothing is being falsified. It is just that the arrangement has taken over the load-bearing work, and words that would once have had to carry a room are now only required not to get in the way.

So the useful thing about voices alone is that it is a test, and a cheap one. Can four people sing this in a kitchen with no instrument and no screen. A song that survives that will survive being sung by a congregation with no band, in a room with no power, and by one person at a graveside who has nothing but the words. A song that does not survive it was never portable, and portability is most of what a hymn is for.
None of which is an argument against production. It is an argument about what production can be asked to tell you.

Because a good arrangement is a real act of craft and a real act of hospitality. It carries people who cannot sing and know it. It makes a shy room brave enough to open its mouth, and it gives a song a body it can travel in. What the arrangement cannot do is answer the question you think you are answering when you are moved. It can tell you that the music worked. It cannot tell you whether the thing being said is true, because it is perfectly capable of producing the whole effect on its own.
Take the arrangement away and the room finds out in about eight seconds.

It is eleven at night in a side room off a ward and a man of seventy-two is singing to his wife, who has not said anything to anybody since Tuesday. He is not a singer. He picks a hymn he learnt at school because it is the only thing that arrives, and he starts too high, and he knows he has started too high and carries on anyway. Halfway through the second verse he gets a line wrong, stops, says sorry out loud to nobody in particular, goes back to the start of the verse and does it again properly. A nurse pauses in the corridor with a chart in her hand and decides not to come in yet. There is no accompaniment, no key, no reverb and no audience, and it is the most that has happened in that room all week.
That is the mechanism. Nothing was carrying those words except the words and a man who meant them, and at eleven at night in a side room that is the only kind of carrying that is available anyway.

It has to be admitted that this is often not pleasant to listen to. Most people cannot really sing, unaccompanied singing exposes that within a bar, and an evening of it would be hard work for a lot of listeners. There is also a dishonest version: the immaculate close-harmony group, stacked and tuned and edited until it gleams. That is production by other means. It has simply moved the studio inside the voices, and it will pass no test at all.

But the roughness is not a defect in the format. It is the format. The purpose of taking the arrangement away is not to produce a nicer listening experience — it plainly does not — but to find out what was there. The unpleasantness is where the information is. A line that still stands up when it is sung flat, in the wrong key, by somebody who is frightened, is a line that will still be standing up in forty years, and that is the property that matters most about a worship song.

This is also, historically, the normal condition rather than a stunt. Almost every song that has lasted more than a century was written for voices and whatever happened to be in the room, and much of the world still worships that way this morning, because that is what is available. The stripped version is not a special edition of the song. It is the song, and everything else is a delivery vehicle.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, 40 frequencies carrying 29 languages between them. All of it runs to a schedule published before it airs, and two people who tune to the same number at the same second hear the same thing.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 306.20 — Hebraic Celebrations. It is Zev Inspire’s feast-day catalogue, Hebraic chant and modern fusion, anchored in Jerusalem, and it is the closest thing on this dial to the argument of this article. Chant is what is left when the production stops. It is carried by a voice, a mode and a room that already knows the words, and it never had a production budget to lose in the first place — the material is older than the recording industry by a distance that makes the question look small. The morning hour at nine is the Shema and the evening hour at six is the Erev Celebration. Put it on and listen to how much is being carried by how little.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built and how the ones already on air get better.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 306.20 on this evening while you are doing the washing up, and then, at some point in the middle of a song, turn it off and carry on singing. That is the whole test and it takes eight seconds. Whatever you can still carry at the sink with nothing behind it is what you actually have, and it will be there on the night the power goes, in a hall with badminton lines on the floor, or in a side room at eleven o’clock when it is the only thing left to do.
